blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 23 (Carbonyl Compounds and Carboxylic Acids), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Describe the laboratory preparation of ethanal from ethanol. Explain the conditions used and how the preparation of a ketone from a secondary alcohol differs. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Principle: aldehydes are prepared by the oxidation of primary alcohols with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ or acidified KMnO₄.
CH₃–CH₂–OH + [O] → CH₃–CHO + H₂O (K₂Cr₂O₇ + H₂SO₄(aq), heat)

Method (Figure 23.1):
• Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ is added drop wise to warm ethanol.
• The ethanal produced is distilled off as soon as it is formed. This prevents its further oxidation to ethanoic acid.
• The temperature is kept above the boiling point of ethanal (acetaldehyde) but below that of ethanol, since ethanol has the higher boiling point; so ethanal distils over and ethanol stays behind.
• Pure ethanal is obtained by redistillation.

Ketones: prepared by the same procedure from secondary alcohols, e.g.
CH₃–CH(OH)–CH₃ + [O] → CH₃–CO–CH₃ + H₂O (propan-2-ol → propanone)
Ketones are not converted into carboxylic acids under these conditions, so the ketone is not distilled off immediately.

book_ref.quote: the acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ is added drop wise to the warm ethanol

blocks.prompt: 2 Explain the structure of the carbonyl group and the two structural features that decide its reactions. Why are aldehydes more reactive than ketones? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Structure: in >C=O both carbon and oxygen are sp² hybridized. Carbon is bonded to oxygen through a double bond (σ + π) and to two other groups through single bonds; the group is planar.
Polarity: oxygen is more electronegative, so it gets a partial negative charge (δ⁻) and carbon a partial positive charge (δ⁺): >C^δ⁺=O^δ⁻.

Two structural features:
1. The carbonyl carbon is electrophilic due to its δ⁺ charge and can be attacked by nucleophiles.
2. The double bond can undergo addition reactions because the π bond is easily broken; the planar shape makes the carbonyl carbon uncrowded, further supporting addition.
So the typical reactions are nucleophilic addition reactions (and α-carbon specific reactions).

Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones:
• Inductive effect: in a ketone the electron releasing effect of two alkyl groups reduces the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon, making it less easily attacked.
• Steric hindrance: the two alkyl groups of a ketone get in the way of the attacking nucleophile.

book_ref.quote: Two structural features of the carbonyl group determine the chemistry and properties

blocks.prompt: 3 Describe the addition of hydrogen cyanide to propanone: how HCN is provided, the role of free CN⁻ ions, the steps of the reaction and the use of the product. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Reaction: aldehydes and ketones react with HCN to form cyanohydrins.
CH₃COCH₃ + HCN → (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN (2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile)

Providing HCN: HCN is an extremely poisonous gas, so it is not used directly. A controlled amount of acid (HCl) is added slowly to a mixture of KCN (or NaCN) solution and the carbonyl compound: KCN + HCl → HCN + KCl.

Role of CN⁻: HCN is neither a nucleophile (no lone pair on its carbon) nor a strong acid, so it does not give enough CN⁻. A slight excess of KCN is used so that free CN⁻ ions are present; they start the reaction and catalyse it at a reasonable rate.

Steps:
1. The nucleophile CN⁻ attacks the δ⁺ carbonyl carbon; the π electrons move to oxygen, giving an alkoxide ion (CH₃)₂C(O⁻)CN.
2. The alkoxide ion takes H⁺ from HCN, giving the cyanohydrin and regenerating CN⁻.
Both steps are reversible but the equilibria lie far to the right, so yields are high.

Use: 2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile is an intermediate in the manufacture of Perspex. Nitriles can be hydrolysed to carboxylic acids.

book_ref.quote: HCN is obtained by adding a controlled amount of an acid to a mixture of KCN and the carbonyl compound.

blocks.prompt: 4 Explain the reduction of aldehydes and ketones by hydride ion. Give the reduction of propanal and of propanone and outline how the hydride ion reacts. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Since aldehydes and ketones are made by oxidising alcohols, alcohols are obtained back by their reduction. With a reducing agent such as NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄ (source of hydride ion, H⁻):
• aldehydes give primary alcohols: CH₃CH₂CHO + 2[H] → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH (propan-1-ol)
• ketones give secondary alcohols: CH₃COCH₃ + 2[H] → CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ (propan-2-ol)
[H] is the reducing H from NaBH₄ written to balance the equation; it does not represent atomic hydrogen.

How the hydride ion reacts (nucleophilic addition):
1. The hydride ion H⁻ (nucleophile) attacks the δ⁺ carbonyl carbon; the π electrons move onto oxygen, forming an alkoxide ion.
2. The alkoxide ion takes H⁺ from water (aqueous solution), giving the alcohol.
Aldehydes react more readily than ketones because the ketone carbon is less δ⁺ and more hindered.

book_ref.quote: alcohols can be produced by the reduction of aldehydes and ketones

blocks.prompt: 5 Describe the reaction of carbonyl compounds with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine. Why is it called a condensation reaction and how is it used? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Reaction: aldehydes and ketones undergo a condensation (addition-elimination) reaction with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH) to give orange crystalline solids with well-defined melting points.
Example: ethanal + 2,4-DNPH → ethanal 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone (orange crystals) + H₂O
CH₃CHO + H₂N–NH–C₆H₃(NO₂)₂ → CH₃CH=N–NH–C₆H₃(NO₂)₂ + H₂O

Why condensation: the –NH₂ group of the reagent first adds to the C=O group (addition) and then a molecule of water is eliminated, joining the two molecules through C=N.

Use:
• The reagent is used to identify carbonyl compounds (aldehydes and ketones): an orange precipitate shows a >C=O group of an aldehyde or ketone.
• The melting point of the crystals helps to identify the particular compound.
• Carboxylic acids, esters, acyl halides and amides also contain >C=O but do not give this test.
Note: 2,4-DNPH is the reagent; the orange crystals are the hydrazone product.

book_ref.quote: Other classes of organic compounds like carboxylic acids, esters, acyl halides, amides etc

blocks.prompt: 6 Describe Tollens' test and Fehling's test with equations. Why do ketones not give these tests? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Aldehydes are easily oxidised by both weak and strong oxidising agents. Ketones are reluctant towards oxidation because a C–C bond has to be broken, so they are oxidised only by strong oxidising agents. Tollens' and Fehling's reagents are weak oxidising agents, so only aldehydes respond.

Tollens' test:
• Reagent: ammoniacal silver nitrate, silver ions in aqueous alkaline solution:
AgNO₃ + 3NH₄OH → [Ag(NH₃)₂]OH + NH₄NO₃ + 2H₂O
• On gentle warming with an aldehyde, Ag⁺ is reduced to silver metal, forming a silver mirror on the wall of the test tube (the aldehyde is oxidised to the acid / its salt). A dilute glucose solution was used this way to make domestic mirrors.

Fehling's test:
• Reagent: bright blue solution of Cu²⁺ ions in aqueous alkaline medium, complexed with a salt of tartaric acid.
• Warmed with an aldehyde, Cu²⁺ is reduced to Cu⁺, which forms a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide:
R–CHO + 2Cu(OH)₂ + NaOH → R–COO⁻Na⁺ + Cu₂O↓ + 3H₂O

Ketones give neither a silver mirror nor a red precipitate.

book_ref.quote: Aldehydes and ketones are oxidized to form carboxylic acids.

blocks.prompt: 7 Which compounds give the iodoform test? Write the iodoform reactions of ethanal and propanone, and explain why ethanol gives the test but methanol does not. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Aldehydes and ketones readily undergo substitution by halogens at the alpha position. Compounds with the CH₃CO– (acetyl / ethanoyl) group – among aldehydes only ethanal, among ketones only methyl ketones – react with iodine in the presence of NaOH to form triiodomethane, CHI₃, a yellow crystalline solid called iodoform. A yellow precipitate identifies the CH₃CO– group.

Ethanal: CH₃CHO + 3I₂ + 4NaOH → CHI₃↓ + HCOO⁻Na⁺ + 3NaI + 3H₂O (sodium methanoate)
Propanone: CH₃COCH₃ + 3I₂ + 4NaOH → CHI₃↓ + CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + 3NaI + 3H₂O (sodium ethanoate)

Ethanol: it has the CH₃–CH(OH)– group. Iodine in alkali first oxidises it to ethanal, CH₃CHO, which has the CH₃–C=O group and then gives iodoform:
CH₃CH₂OH + 4I₂ + 6NaOH → CHI₃ + HCOONa + 5NaI + 5H₂O
Methanol cannot give a compound with a CH₃–C=O group, so it gives no iodoform.

book_ref.quote: Thus it can also form iodoform, and the test is positive for ethanol.

blocks.prompt: 8 What are carboxylic acids? Give three examples with their sources and explain their physical properties (boiling point, glacial acetic acid, solubility, fatty acids). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Carboxylic acids are organic compounds having the carboxyl functional group, –COOH (general structure R–COOH).
Examples: methanoic acid (formic acid, found in ants); ethanoic acid (acetic acid, found in vinegar); butanoic acid (butyric acid, in rancid butter).

Physical properties:
• Boiling points: lower carboxylic acids are liquids at room temperature with high boiling points, due to hydrogen bonding; two molecules of acetic acid join as a hydrogen-bonded dimer.
• Glacial acetic acid: ethanoic acid melts at 17 °C and boils at 118 °C. Its melting point is close to room temperature (25 °C), so it solidifies in winter; the solid pure acid resembles glaciers and is called glacial acetic acid.
• Solubility: due to hydrogen bonding with water, the lower acids (methanoic and ethanoic acid) are soluble in water.
• Fatty acids: long chain aliphatic monocarboxylic acids, e.g. stearic, palmitic (C₁₆H₃₂O₂, in palm oil) and oleic acids, found in vegetable oils as triglycerides. They are insoluble in water due to their long hydrophobic alkyl chains.

book_ref.quote: Lower carboxylic acids are generally liquids at room temperature, having high boiling points.

blocks.prompt: 9 How do the conditions of oxidation decide whether a primary alcohol gives an aldehyde or a carboxylic acid? Describe the preparation of ethanoic acid from ethanol and of benzoic acid from methylbenzene. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
A primary alcohol is oxidised first to an aldehyde and then to a carboxylic acid; the conditions decide where it stops:

Benzoic acid (benzenecarboxylic acid): methylbenzene is readily oxidised by acidified KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇; the –CH₃ side chain becomes –COOH:
C₆H₅CH₃ + 3[O] → C₆H₅COOH + H₂O

book_ref.quote: Carboxylic acids are prepared by the oxidation of primary alcohols and aldehydes.

rows: Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ added drop wise to warm alcohol
Refluxed with excess acidified KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇
Aldehyde distilled off as soon as formed
Aldehyde stays in the hot mixture (reflux)

blocks.prompt: 10 Explain how ethanoic acid is obtained by hydrolysis of (i) ethanenitrile and (ii) ethyl ethanoate, in acidic and in alkaline medium. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Hydrolysis of ethanenitrile (an alkane nitrile)
• Acidic medium: hydrolysed directly to the carboxylic acid:
CH₃CN + 2H₂O + HCl → CH₃COOH + NH₄Cl
• Alkaline medium: first gives the salt of the acid, which gives the acid on acidification:
CH₃CN + NaOH + H₂O → CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + NH₃
CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + HCl → CH₃COOH + NaCl

(ii) Hydrolysis of ethyl ethanoate (an ester), refluxed with dilute acid or dilute alkali
• Acidic medium (reversible): CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH
• Alkaline medium: CH₃COOC₂H₅ + NaOH → CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + C₂H₅OH
With NaOH the acid formed becomes its salt, so the reaction goes to completion (one-way arrow); acidification of the salt gives ethanoic acid:
CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + HCl → CH₃COOH + NaCl

book_ref.quote: When an ester is refluxed with either dilute acid or dilute alkali

blocks.prompt: 11 Why do carboxylic acids show acidic character? Write the reactions of ethanoic acid with an active metal, an alkali, a metal carbonate and a metal bicarbonate. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Carboxylic acids show considerable acidic character because they give H⁺ ions in water:
CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺
So they react with basic species and active metals (reactions involving the acidic hydrogen only).

(a) With an active metal: 2CH₃COOH + 2Na → 2CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + H₂ (hydrogen gas evolved)
(b) With an alkali: CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + H₂O (neutralisation)
(c) With a metal carbonate: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + CO₂ + H₂O
(d) With a metal bicarbonate: CH₃COOH + NaHCO₃ → CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + CO₂ + H₂O
In (c) and (d) carbon dioxide is given off with effervescence. In every case the salt formed is sodium ethanoate.

book_ref.quote: This why they can react with the basic species and active metals.

blocks.prompt: 12 Describe the reactions of carboxylic acids in which the –OH group is replaced (by Cl and by OR), and the reduction of the –COOH group. Name a reducing agent that fails. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Replacement of –OH: carboxylic acids undergo substitution reactions in which the –OH group is replaced by another group such as X, OR or NH₂.

(a) By Cl – with SOCl₂, PCl₃ or PCl₅, giving an acyl chloride:
CH₃COOH + SOCl₂ → CH₃COCl + HCl + SO₂
CH₃COOH + PCl₅ → CH₃COCl + HCl + POCl₃

(b) By OR – esterification: heating with an alcohol in the presence of concentrated H₂SO₄ gives an ester (reversible):
CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O (ethyl ethanoate)

Reduction of –COOH: the powerful reducing agent lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III), LiAlH₄, reduces carboxylic acids to primary alcohols:
CH₃COOH + 4[H] → CH₃CH₂OH + H₂O
Other common reducing agents, H₂/Ni and sodium tetrahydridoborate(III) (NaBH₄), will not reduce carboxylic acids.

book_ref.quote: Carboxylic acids can undergo substitution reactions in which the OH group is replaced

blocks.prompt: 13 Explain why methanoic acid behaves as a reducing agent and write its reactions with Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution. Also give the oxidation of ethanedioic acid. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Methanoic acid, H–COOH, has an aldehydic portion (H–C=O) as well as a carboxylic portion (–COOH). Due to this structure it is oxidised by both weak and strong oxidising agents and so acts as a strong reducing agent.

It is the only monocarboxylic acid that gives a silver mirror (Tollens' test) and a brick-red precipitate with Fehling's solution; these reactions identify methanoic acid:
H–COOH + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]OH → 2Ag↓ + CO₂ + 4NH₃ + 2H₂O (silver mirror)
H–COOH + 2Cu(OH)₂ → Cu₂O↓ + CO₂ + 3H₂O (brick red ppt)

Ethanedioic acid: oxidised by acidified KMnO₄ (or K₂Cr₂O₇) to carbon dioxide and water:
2KMnO₄ + 3H₂SO₄ + 5HOOC–COOH → K₂SO₄ + 2MnSO₄ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O
Mn changes from +7 to +2 (reduced) and C from +3 to +4 (oxidised).

book_ref.quote: These reactions are used for the identification of methanoic acid.

blocks.prompt: 14 For the reaction 2KMnO₄ + 3H₂SO₄ + 5H₂C₂O₄ → K₂SO₄ + 2MnSO₄ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O: (i) find the oxidation numbers of Mn and C before and after the reaction and show that the electrons lost equal the electrons gained; (ii) calculate the moles of KMnO₄ needed and of CO₂ formed for 0.25 mol of ethanedioic acid. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find oxidation numbers from the formulas (K = +1, O = –2, H = +1), count electrons per atom times atoms, then use the mole ratio of the balanced equation.

book_ref.quote: results in the formation of carbon dioxide and water

steps: Mn in KMnO₄: +1 + x + 4(–2) = 0, x = +7; Mn in MnSO₄: x + (–2) = 0 (SO₄²⁻ carries –2), x = +2. Mn gains 5 electrons.
C in H₂C₂O₄: 2(+1) + 2y + 4(–2) = 0, y = +3; C in CO₂: y + 2(–2) = 0, y = +4. Each C loses 1 electron.
Electrons gained by 2 Mn = 2 × 5 = 10; electrons lost by 10 C (in 5 H₂C₂O₄) = 10 × 1 = 10. Lost = gained, so the equation is balanced in electrons.
blocks.final_answer: Mn +7 → +2, C +3 → +4; 10 electrons transferred; KMnO₄ = 0.10 mol, CO₂ = 0.50 mol

blocks.prompt: 15 Explain, on the basis of the stability of the conjugate base, why carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenols and alcohols. How do +I and –I groups affect the acidity? Use methanoic and ethanoic acids as an example. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Order of acidity (Table 23.1): RCOOH (Ka 10⁻⁵, pKa 5) > ArOH (10⁻¹⁰, 10) > HOH (10⁻¹⁴, 14) > R–OH (10⁻¹⁶, 16). Since pKa = –log Ka, higher Ka or lower pKa means a stronger acid.

Conjugate base: the extent of ionization of an acid depends on the stability of its conjugate base.
CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺
In the ethanoate ion the negative charge is delocalised over the –COO⁻ group (the carbon and both oxygen atoms), so the intensity of negative charge on oxygen decreases. The stabilised ion is less likely to accept H⁺ to form the undissociated acid, so the acid ionises more.

Effect of substituents:
• An electron donating group (+I) intensifies the negative charge, destabilises the carboxylate ion and decreases acidity.
• An electron withdrawing group (–I) disperses the negative charge, stabilises the carboxylate ion and increases acidity.

Example: methanoic acid is about 10 times stronger than ethanoic acid. Hydrogen is the reference and has no –I effect; the CH₃ group of ethanoic acid has a +I effect, which destabilises ethanoate.

book_ref.quote: making it less likely to accept H⁺ ions to form undissociated acid molecule

blocks.prompt: 16 Three carboxylic acids have Ka values: acid A 6.3 × 10⁻⁵, acid B 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, acid C 3.2 × 10⁻³; a phenol has Ka 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰. Calculate the pKa of each, arrange them in order of decreasing acid strength, and find how many times stronger acid C is than acid B. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use pKa = –log Ka; the lower the pKa (higher Ka), the stronger the acid; compare strengths by the ratio of Ka values.

book_ref.quote: The relative values of acidity constant or ionization constant, Ka

steps: Lowest pKa is strongest: C (2.49) > A (4.20) > B (4.74) > phenol (10.00)
Ka(C) / Ka(B) = 3.2 × 10⁻³ / 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ = 178, so C is about 1.8 × 10² times stronger than B.
blocks.final_answer: pKa: A 4.20, B 4.74, C 2.49, phenol 10.00; order C > A > B > phenol; C is about 178 times stronger than B

blocks.prompt: 17 The pKa values of ethanoic acid, chloroethanoic acid, dichloroethanoic acid and trichloroethanoic acid are 4.74, 2.86, 1.26 and 0.64. Calculate the Ka of each acid, find how many times stronger trichloroethanoic acid is than ethanoic acid, and explain the trend. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Ka = 10^–pKa; the ratio of two Ka values is 10 raised to the difference of their pKa values; explain with the –I effect of Cl.

book_ref.quote: Dichloroethanoic acid (Cl₂CH-COOH) is stronger, with a pKa of 1.26

steps: Trend: each Cl atom has a –I effect that disperses the negative charge of the carboxylate ion and stabilises it; more Cl atoms give more stabilisation, a larger Ka and a lower pKa. Trichloroethanoic acid is comparable to some mineral acids.
blocks.final_answer: Ka: 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, 1.4 × 10⁻³, 5.5 × 10⁻², 2.3 × 10⁻¹; trichloroethanoic acid is about 1.3 × 10⁴ times stronger than ethanoic acid

blocks.prompt: 18 What are esters? Explain their physical properties in terms of hydrogen bonding and give their uses. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Esters are derivatives of carboxylic acids obtained by their reactions with alcohols, e.g. ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOC₂H₅.

Physical properties:
• Hydrogen bonding: unlike alcohols and carboxylic acids, esters have no ability to form hydrogen bonds among their molecules.
• Boiling point: therefore their boiling points are lower than those of the corresponding alcohols and carboxylic acids. Ethyl ethanoate boils at 77 °C (ethanoic acid 118 °C); a lower boiling point means a higher volatility, so the ester is more volatile.
• Solubility: lack of hydrogen bonds makes esters less soluble or insoluble in water.
• Smell: many (volatile) esters are liquids with sweet fruity smells; the fragrance and taste of fruits are due to esters.

Uses: as solvents, and as flavouring agents in fruit drinks and sweets.

book_ref.quote: Esters, unlike alcohols and carboxylic acids have no ability to form the hydrogen bond.

blocks.prompt: 19 Describe the methods of preparing esters from (i) a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, (ii) an acyl chloride and an alcohol, (iii) an acyl chloride and phenol. Also write the hydrolysis of an aromatic ester. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Carboxylic acid + alcohol (Fischer's esterification): in acidic medium (conc. H₂SO₄) an ester and water form; the reaction is an equilibrium.
CH₃CH₂COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃CH₂COOC₂H₅ + H₂O (ethyl propanoate)
In general: RCOOH + R'OH ⇌ RCOOR' + H₂O (the –OH of the acid and the H of the alcohol leave as water).

(ii) Acyl chloride + alcohol: reacts vigorously; the reaction goes to completion and does not form an equilibrium mixture.
CH₃COCl + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + HCl (ethyl ethanoate)

(iii) Acyl chloride + phenol: phenyl esters are formed when an acyl chloride is warmed with phenol.
CH₃COCl + C₆H₅OH → CH₃COOC₆H₅ + HCl (phenyl ethanoate)

Hydrolysis: an ester is hydrolysed slowly (acid- or base-catalysed) to a carboxylic acid and an alcohol (or phenol); aromatic esters behave the same way:
C₆H₅COOC₂H₅ + H₂O → C₆H₅COOH + C₂H₅OH (ethyl benzoate → benzoic acid + ethanol)

book_ref.quote: Acyl chlorides react vigorously with alcohols to form esters and their reactions go to completion

blocks.prompt: 20 What are acyl chlorides? Give their general formula and naming, how they are prepared from carboxylic acids, and why they are used to make other derivatives, with two reactions. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Acyl chlorides have the functional group –COCl. Saturated aliphatic acyl chlorides have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COCl. In the IUPAC system they are named alkanoyl halides: CH₃COCl ethanoyl chloride, CH₃CH₂COCl propanoyl chloride.

Preparation: the –OH of a carboxylic acid is replaced by Cl using SOCl₂, PCl₃ or PCl₅:
CH₃COOH + SOCl₂ → CH₃COCl + HCl + SO₂
CH₃COOH + PCl₅ → CH₃COCl + HCl + POCl₃

Reactivity and use: acyl chlorides are the most reactive of the functional derivatives of carboxylic acids (the carbonyl carbon carries a large δ⁺ because O and Cl both withdraw electrons), so they are prepared in order to make other derivatives:
• with an alcohol (goes to completion): CH₃COCl + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + HCl
• with water (within minutes): CH₃COCl + H₂O → CH₃COOH + HCl
• with phenol on warming: phenyl esters.

book_ref.quote: Since acyl chlorides are the most reactive compounds among the functional derivatives of carboxylic acids

blocks.prompt: 21 Ethanoyl chloride, chloroethane and chlorobenzene are each treated with water. Write the equations where reaction occurs, and justify the order of their ease of hydrolysis from their structures. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Order of ease of hydrolysis: ethanoyl chloride > chloroethane > chlorobenzene (no reaction). In each case water acts as a nucleophile attacking a δ⁺ carbon.

Ethanoyl chloride: CH₃COCl + H₂O → CH₃COOH + HCl
The carbonyl carbon is attached to two highly electronegative atoms, O and Cl, whose strong electron withdrawing effect gives it a large δ⁺. Nucleophilic attack of H₂O is so fast that the reaction is complete within a few minutes.

Chloroethane: C₂H₅Cl + H₂O → C₂H₅OH + HCl
The carbon is attached to only one chlorine atom, so it has comparatively less δ⁺. The attack of water is slow and the mixture must be heated for a long time.

Chlorobenzene: no hydrolysis.
The C–Cl carbon is part of the benzene ring. A lone pair on chlorine takes part in delocalisation with the π electrons of the ring, giving the C–Cl bond double bond character. The bond becomes so strong that it does not break.

book_ref.quote: Here, lone pair on chlorine participates in delocalization with π electrons of the benzene ring.

rows: Fastest (minutes): C attached to O and Cl, large δ⁺
Slow (needs heating): C attached to Cl only, less δ⁺
No reaction: C–Cl has double bond character
